parts: Lesson 4: Cooperative Societies and Joint Stock Companies — Summary

A voluntary association of persons who join together to protect and promote their common economic interests on the basis of equality and mutual help. Its main aim is service to members, not profit. Example: Amul (Gujarat Cooperative Milk Marketing Federation), owned by lakhs of milk producers.

Characteristics: voluntary membership — anyone can join or leave; open membership irrespective of caste or religion; registration is compulsory (Cooperative Societies Act, 1912, or state Acts), with a minimum of ten members; separate legal entity and stable life — death, insolvency or insanity of members does not affect it; limited liability of members; democratic management — 'one man, one vote' whatever the number of shares; service motive; capital raised mainly from members' shares; surplus distributed as limited dividend and bonus on purchases.

Types: consumers' cooperatives (Kendriya Bhandar, Apna Bazar, Super Bazar — buy directly from producers and sell to members at fair prices); producers' cooperatives (handloom societies — supply raw materials and tools to small producers); marketing cooperatives (Amul — collect and sell members' products); thrift and credit cooperatives (village service societies, urban cooperative banks — accept deposits and give cheap loans); cooperative housing societies (build or buy houses for members at reasonable cost); cooperative farming societies.

Advantages: easy formation; limited liability; stable life; democratic control; service at low cost by eliminating middlemen; government help (loans, tax relief). Limitations: limited capital; inefficient management by honorary office-bearers; members lack zeal because they get only limited dividend and no extra reward for effort; conflicts among members; excessive government regulation; lack of secrecy.

A voluntary association of persons formed under the Companies Act, with a capital divided into transferable shares. Characteristics: artificial legal person created by law; separate legal entity — it can own property, sue and be sued in its own name; perpetual succession — members may come and go but the company continues; common seal; limited liability of shareholders to the unpaid value of their shares; transferability of shares (free in a public company); separation of ownership and management — shareholders own it, elected directors manage it; registration under the Companies Act is compulsory.

Private company: minimum 2 members (maximum 200 under the 2013 Act; 50 earlier), restrictions on transfer of shares, cannot invite the public to buy shares, at least 2 directors. Public company: minimum 7 members, no maximum, shares freely transferable, can issue a prospectus, at least 3 directors (e.g. Reliance Industries Ltd). Advantages: large capital; limited liability; perpetual succession; transferability of shares; professional management; scope for expansion and research. Limitations: difficult and costly formation; excessive legal control; lack of secrecy; delay in decisions; separation of ownership and control can lead to misuse by directors; conflict of interests.

A company in which at least 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the central or a state government (or both). Examples: Coal India, ONGC, Indian Oil Corporation, SAIL, NTPC, MTNL. Features: separate legal entity registered under the Companies Act; all or most directors are appointed by the government; its accounts are audited under the Comptroller and Auditor General and the reports go to Parliament; it gets its funds from government and the public.

A company with its head office in one country and business operations (factories, branches, offices) in many countries — Hindustan Unilever, Nestle, Samsung, Coca-Cola, Hyundai, Suzuki. Advantages to the host country: inflow of foreign capital, latest technology, employment, better quality goods and wider choice, export promotion and foreign exchange, competition that pushes domestic producers to improve quality, and professional management. Limitations: they may harm small domestic industries, send large profits abroad, interfere in local politics, exploit natural resources and spread a foreign consumer culture.
